assignments.title: Homework 1: Stack and Queue Implementation
assignments.content:
CS 201 -- Homework 1: Stack and Queue Implementation
Due: September 19, 2026, 11:59 PM
Points: 50

Overview
--------
Implement a generic Stack and a generic Queue from scratch using a singly
linked list as the underlying storage. You may NOT use Python's built-in
list, collections.deque, or any other built-in container to store the
elements -- the point of this assignment is the linked-list mechanics, not
the public interface.

Requirements
------------
1. Implement class Stack with push(item), pop(), peek(), and is_empty().
   pop() and peek() on an empty stack must raise IndexError with a clear
   message, not crash with an unrelated exception.
2. Implement class Queue with enqueue(item), dequeue(), peek(), and
   is_empty(), with the same empty-queue error handling as Stack.
3. Both classes must run in O(1) time for every operation above. If your
   Queue's dequeue() is O(n), you have almost certainly chosen the wrong
   end of the list to remove from -- revisit the lecture notes on
   head/tail pointers before asking on the forum.
4. Write at least 5 unit tests per class covering: normal operation,
   popping/dequeuing down to empty, and the empty-container error case.

Submission
----------
Submit a single file named hw1_<your_student_id>.py through the course
portal. Late submissions lose 10% per day, up to 3 days; nothing is
accepted after that without a documented excuse cleared with the
instructor in advance.

Grading breakdown
------------------
- Stack implementation and correctness: 15 pts
- Queue implementation and correctness: 15 pts
- O(1) complexity (checked via a provided timing harness): 10 pts
- Unit tests: 10 pts

assignments.title: Homework 2: Binary Search Tree Operations
assignments.content:
CS 201 -- Homework 2: Binary Search Tree Operations
Due: October 10, 2026, 11:59 PM
Points: 75

Overview
--------
Build a Binary Search Tree (BST) supporting insert, search, delete, and an
in-order traversal that returns a sorted list of the tree's values.

Requirements
------------
1. insert(value): standard BST insertion; duplicate values should be
   ignored (do not insert a second copy, and do not raise an error).
2. search(value) -> bool: returns whether value exists in the tree.
3. delete(value): must correctly handle all three cases -- a leaf node,
   a node with one child, and a node with two children (use the
   in-order successor for the two-child case, as covered in lecture).
4. inorder() -> list: returns all values in sorted order.
5. height() -> int: returns the tree's height; an empty tree has height
   -1, a single-node tree has height 0.

A provided test harness (bst_harness.py, posted on the course portal)
will insert 500 random integers, delete 100 of them, and check that
inorder() stays sorted and search() stays consistent throughout. Your
submission must pass this harness without modification to pass.

Submission
----------
Submit bst_<your_student_id>.py through the course portal. This
assignment builds directly on Homework 1's linked-node style -- reuse
your own Node class pattern rather than starting from scratch.

Grading breakdown
------------------
- insert/search: 20 pts
- delete (all three cases): 30 pts
- inorder/height: 15 pts
- Passes the provided harness end-to-end: 10 pts

assignments.title: Homework 3: Graph Traversal (BFS/DFS)
assignments.content:
CS 201 -- Homework 3: Graph Traversal (BFS/DFS)
Due: November 7, 2026, 11:59 PM
Points: 75

Overview
--------
Implement both breadth-first search (BFS) and depth-first search (DFS)
over a graph represented as an adjacency list, and use them to answer
two practical questions about the graph.

Requirements
------------
1. Represent the graph as dict[node, list[node]] -- build a small loader
   that reads an edge list from a text file (one 'A B' pair per line)
   into this representation. Treat the graph as undirected unless a
   line is prefixed with '>' (directed A -> B only).
2. bfs(graph, start) -> list: returns nodes in visiting order.
3. dfs(graph, start) -> list: returns nodes in visiting order
   (iterative, using an explicit stack -- do NOT use recursion, to
   avoid Python's recursion limit on larger graphs).
4. shortest_path(graph, start, end) -> list | None: using BFS, return
   the shortest path as a list of nodes, or None if unreachable.
5. is_connected(graph) -> bool: true if every node is reachable from
   every other node (treat the graph as undirected for this check,
   even if it has directed edges).

Test graphs (small.txt, medium.txt, disconnected.txt) are posted on the
course portal along with expected outputs for shortest_path on each.

Submission
----------
Submit graphs_<your_student_id>.py. Include a short README.txt (plain
text, no formatting needed) stating the time complexity of each of the
four functions above in terms of |V| and |E|.

Grading breakdown
------------------
- Graph loader: 10 pts
- BFS/DFS correctness: 30 pts
- shortest_path correctness: 20 pts
- is_connected correctness: 10 pts
- Complexity README: 5 pts

assignments.title: Project 1: Requirements Document and Use-Case Diagrams
assignments.content:
CS 301 -- Project 1: Requirements Document and Use-Case Diagrams
Due: September 26, 2026, 11:59 PM
Points: 100 (team grade)

Overview
--------
In teams of 3-4, pick ONE of the three provided problem statements
(campus parking reservation, dorm maintenance ticketing, or club event
sign-ups) and produce a requirements document for it.

Deliverables
------------
1. A requirements document (PDF, max 6 pages) containing:
   a. Project scope: one paragraph stating what the system will and
      will NOT do.
   b. At least 8 functional requirements, each with a unique ID
      (FR-1, FR-2, ...), written as 'The system shall ...' statements.
   c. At least 3 non-functional requirements (performance, security,
      usability, etc.), each with a unique ID (NFR-1, ...).
   d. A glossary of any domain-specific terms used.
2. At least 3 use-case diagrams (UML notation), covering your three
   most important user-facing scenarios. Hand-drawn diagrams are fine
   if scanned clearly -- a messy photo that can't be read will be
   graded as missing.
3. A one-page team contribution statement: who wrote which sections,
   signed (typed name is fine) by every team member.

Common mistakes from past semesters
------------------------------------
- Writing implementation details ('the system shall use a MySQL
  database') instead of requirements ('the system shall persist
  reservations across sessions'). Requirements describe WHAT, not HOW.
- Use cases that are really just button-click sequences rather than
  actual user goals.
- Skipping the non-functional requirements entirely, or writing vague
  ones like 'the system shall be fast' with no measurable threshold.

Submission
----------
One submission per team through the course portal, team name in the
filename. Team formation is due one week before this deadline --
unassigned students will be placed into a team by the instructor.

Grading breakdown
------------------
- Scope and functional requirements: 35 pts
- Non-functional requirements: 20 pts
- Use-case diagrams: 30 pts
- Contribution statement completeness: 15 pts

assignments.title: Project 2: Design Patterns Code Review
assignments.content:
CS 301 -- Project 2: Design Patterns Code Review
Due: October 24, 2026, 11:59 PM
Points: 80 (individual grade)

Overview
--------
You are given a ~600-line Python codebase (patterns_review_starter.zip,
on the course portal) that works correctly but was written without any
consideration for maintainability. Your job is to refactor it using at
least THREE of the design patterns covered in lecture (Strategy,
Observer, Factory, Decorator, Singleton, Adapter) and document why each
one was the right fit.

Requirements
------------
1. The refactored code must pass the existing test suite
   (test_starter.py) UNCHANGED -- you may not edit the tests to make
   your refactor pass.
2. For each pattern you apply, write a short section (half a page max)
   in PATTERNS.md explaining:
   a. Which specific code smell or duplication the pattern addressed.
   b. Why that pattern specifically, and not one of the others covered
      in lecture.
   c. A before/after snippet (a few lines each, not the whole file).
3. Do not introduce a pattern just to hit the count of three -- a
   pattern applied where it doesn't actually help will lose points,
   not gain them.

What we are actually grading
-----------------------------
This assignment is graded on judgment, not pattern-counting. A
submission with two well-justified, well-applied patterns will score
higher than one with three forced, unnecessary ones.

Submission
----------
Submit a zip containing your refactored source and PATTERNS.md through
the course portal. Include your name and student ID at the top of
PATTERNS.md.

Grading breakdown
------------------
- Test suite still passes unmodified: 15 pts (required to receive any
  further credit on this assignment)
- Pattern selection and justification: 40 pts
- Code quality of the refactor itself: 25 pts
